This has got to be the most innovative strategy game on the market. The decision and relationships mechanics are a stroke of genius, and you will quickly find yourself building up both rapport and enmity with your colleagues as they collaborate with and against you (and you them). Will you be Hitler's boy and ignore the bleating of the spineless von Brauchitsch, or will you enlist Brauchitsch's aid to undermine the will of the Fuhrer and follow the Wehrmacht's own plans for the invasion? Will you endorse the murderous policies of Himmler, and all the trouble they entail for your rear area, or will you vehemently oppose the Einsatzgruppen lest you find yourself before a war crimes tribunal? How about Goebbels and his propaganda news crews? Do you bathe in the spotlight like Rommel, or do you cast them from your command tent with undisguised contempt? You'll have to deal with all these matters and more, all whilst establishing positive working relationships with your army group commanders, and not forgetting Generals Gercke and Wagner - they're in charge of your supply trains and truck columns respectively, and unfortunately for you they have a habit of clashing with your senior commanders (and each other!). If all that wasn't enough of a headache, there's still the matter of actually fighting the campaign. Carry out swift encirclements, dogged defences, and desperate counter attacks all whilst the brutal Russian winter creeps ever closer.

And that's only half the game! You can, of course, also play as Uncle Joe himself; grappling with your own crippling paranoia and casually executing any upstart Marshal who so much as looks at you ♥♥♥♥-eyed. Trade land for time as you throw countless conscript divisions into the path of the advancing Wehrmacht, whilst you build up your mobile forces for an overwhelming counter-attack that will sweep the fascist beast from the Motherland once and for all. And if your Generals don't show the requisite fighting spirit that all good communists should possess? Well, you can always dispatch old Nikita Khrushchev out to the front to instil the necessary backbone.

Every military strategy buff should have this game in their collection. The idea behind it is inspired and the execution is sublime. There is an enormous amount of depth here, but it's far easier to dive into than WWII epics like War in the East or Hearts of Iron. Be warned though, like the aforementioned games it is also very hard indeed. However, there are more than enough customisation options at the start of the game to perfectly tailor the challenge to suit your own tastes.

If you ever dreamed of a War in the East game which is dumbed down, repeated Goebbelsian narratives on the asiatic hordes, claiming the only competent officers in the Soviet army (in 1941, no less) were Tsarist officers, determined to whitewash the Wehrmacht and relied on massive AI cheating to present even a semblance of difficulty, then you STILL will be disappointed with DC:B.

When you take of the role of Franz Halder. the man in charge of the OKH, you face a truly horrifying threat; but not of the Soviet Army. No, your main opponent will be unclear results of your decisions made in the true heart of the game: the unholy union of oddly CYOA-like choices repeated ad nauseam and enigmatic rules governing the war-game gameplay. Will you capture the oil train at the beginning of your campaign or will you not to not give the Soviets a warning of things to come? It's rather difficult to make a call either way, as you know neither the risks nor benefits of any decision you make until you choose it (and make a percentile roll too, for good measure). For how long will you have non-combat formations on mop-up detail? A month? A week or two? Will you immediately have them fight partisans? What do any of these options actually do and what do the various nazis think of the choices? Only through trial-and-error will you ever find out. Perhaps you will even decide to turn off these time-wasters and focus on the wargame you paid big bucks for, only to come to the most horrific conclusion of all: it's mediocre at the best of times and it never is the best of times. The combat values of any counter on the map is entirely unclear and seems to be the exact same thing as the division size. The vaunted logistic system that the game is built around is a joke, as it only matters for the four armoured groups of the Wehrmacht. The Soviet army and infantry of the Wehrmacht are supplied by the Heavens themselves, to the point the former are entirely unbothered about encirclements (not that the Soviet counters will ever get a chance to even use all their supply, as they never reinforce and die faster than flies).

When you grow bored of smacking your two or three hundred abstract size unit blobs against similarly sized blobs of Soviet troops, you might decide: "by golly, I wonder how it is for the Soviet player?". You will start a campaign as Stalin's psychic (not even the designers themselves know who the Soviet player is supposed to be, my guess being the spirit of the immortal science of Marxism-Leninism) and be shocked when the fiddly logistic system, the main opponent of the German player when played by a human is gleefully ignored by the AI. Crossing theatre borders? No consequence. No fuel? No problem! The german army headquarters decided to vacation in the Baltic 600 kilometers from the frontline? Their units don't seem to mind that the officers are away and cheerfully ignore the crippling limitations that you would endure had you be in control. You will realize that you have no clue whether the lines you are forming are strong or weak (they are weak, BTW). Defending as the Soviet Union in June 1941 is a noob trap, you need to go on the offensive in order for your counters to have any appreciable combat value.

I won't comment on the writers blatant clean-Wehrmacht-esque fantasies or the way they dehumanize every single Soviet character in the game to the point that they refuse to treat any named soviet characters save for Stalin (nothing more than a paranoid, megalomaniacal moron), Khrushchyov (a comic book villain who shoots his minions when they displease him) and Zhukov (Stalin's loyalist, but bears the distinction of being the ONLY soviet officer not being continuously decried as utterly corrupt and incompetent) as anything other than subhuman vermin. Where nazi officers get polite, respectful biographies detailing just how brilliant they were, the soviet officers don't even get accurate portraits (as after all, they are the same replacable, subhuman, asiatic filth is the implication), let alone anything but a name and insulting quality (bootlicker, idiot, bootlicking idiot, 'Tsarist'???).

If you want a light wargame, stick to Panzer Corps or SSI games. If you want a serious wargame about the Eastern Front, get Gary Grigsby's War in the East. If you want a narrative experience with your game, pick up any RPG. If you want to indulge in your deeply held belief in the superiority of German strategy, then there is also probably a better game for you elsewhere at a tenth of the cost and double the quality of this one. There is no niche in which this game is worth its outrageous price.

Overall the game is good, mechanics-wise, if you're looking for a dumbed down version of Gary Grigsby's War In the East (i.e. the absolute best in the genre). Moreover, the whole political layer is engaging, adding an interesting spin to the operational level wargames' formula.

What is absolutely revolting though is the disgusting portrayal of the Wehrmacht via Hugo's fictional war diary entries. His unit's commander is repeatedly portrayed as a bumbling drunkard buffoon, while the soldiers commit atrocities on a daily basis - killing old women in the street for no reason, shooting peasants in the legs to make them dance and even engaging in acts of zoophilia by raping sheep in broad daylight and in view of the entire unit. Mind you this is not the Einsatzgruppen or a penal battalion but a regular German division whose men are portrayed as the evil, incompetent brutes that every Hollywood WWII 'movie' has made them look for decades. This is not entertaining fiction but grotesque propaganda.

VR Designs, your bias is showing. Kindly fxck off.

This game is a good middle ground between beer-and-pretzels wargaming and the hardcore counter shuffling of War in the East 2. What distinguishes it from other wargames is its relationship system, which adds an RPG layer to the counter shuffling. 

I'd love to see a version of this system where you can't micro the individual units at all, but have to issue directives and assign objectives at the army level through the relationship system. This system could easily be expanded beyond Barbarossa to cover the entire war in the east. The interpersonal issues that plagued the German command during Barbarossa persisted until the end of the war. 

I am pretty low-time in this game and will probably stay that way because the counter shuffling phase of the game hasn't grabbed me (I'd rather shuffle counters in War in the East 2). But overall this is a great take on operational level wargaming and I would recommend giving it a try. It is an excellent title for someone who wants to test the hex and counter waters before diving into more intimidating titles.

I would like to compare this game with the 'advanced tactics: golden version'.  
(Background: I played ATG over 300 hours. There is a similar scenario of Barbarossa in ATG, where I usually played Soviet and could win the AI++. When playing this game, I did not read the manual. Of course, I lost the game. I tried twice, both lost. Then I read the game manual, and understand the point of this game.) 

Brief summary: 
On the combat level, they are nearly the same, except a few algorithms. 
On the supply level, they are completely different. This game is a role-player game: you have many 'constraints' from your role, except that this is a role in war game rather. ATG is a total war game: you are less constrained and you are in full control of the war. 

Details: (mostly viewed from the Soviet side. )
(1) Strength of your units.
In this game, the key concept is Activation & Threat. You have to rely on the two troubleshooters to improve the strength of your units. You can only do this on the army HQ and the front HQ level. The operations are limited. Half your time is spent on this side. 
On ATG, it is simplified. You just need to produce enough Staff into your HQ. The number of Staff is equivalent to the above Activation measures. 
(2) Supply. 
In this game, if you are playing Germany, you have to design your supply line by building railway stations and adopting trucks. The other half of your time is spent on this side. 
On ATG, supply is mostly determined by your production. The supply obtained by the front-line units are determined by the size of their HQ. (Of course, their are railway and trucks, but they are not the key factors.) 

(3) Production. 
As metioned above, in ATG you have to manipulate production: city workers, war factories, natural resources. This is the key factor in ATG. And this makes ATG a game of total war. In this game, there is no production control. So this game is only a role-playing game. 

(4) Deal with divisions. 
In ATG, you can do detailed operations on the division level. You can change the weapons of each division. You can disband any amount of division in each turn. You can recreate any amount of division using your production. You can make new HQ. 
In this game, you can not do any detailed operation on the division. You have less freedom in the combat. 

(5) AI. 
The AI in this game is more powerful. In ATG, the AI will leave many troops behind in big cities. But you can choose AI++, where the computer has 250% production over you. Then the army in the front-line overwelms you. You can still feel the challenge. 

Summary: 
These is my understanding of their difference, the difference of their key factors. As a role-playing game,  the interaction among computer army Generals leads to the random outcome to this game. This is lacked in ATG. Most of the concepts are the same, like strength, combat, and supply. They only differ in detailed implementation and operation. However, in ATG, there are the production and division-level manipulation, which are lacked in this game.

My buddy got me into playing these wargames. I came back to try this after having played DC: Ardennes which had a much deeper focus on the nitty gritty of combat.

This feels like I'm playing a WW2 Political Party version of "The View" while trying to manage a campaign, and it's great fun. Most RTS and even strategy games forget the important yet frustrating layers of  warfare - and this keeps you fully rooted in that reality.

An army doesn't move without trucks or trains and the people in charge of both hate each other, and hate you. Your chief of staff can hamstring your efforts. The dude who runs the air force is a giant baby. The guy in control of Germany is an even bigger baby without any military acumen - and he's giving you orders.

On the other hand, Uncle Joe is deeply paranoid and kills everyone around him of actual use, leaving you to defend a full on invasion with whoever is brave enough to stick their head up to get it chopped off.

I had played similar games based on this engine and I must say, engine is definitely bugged when it comes to logistics. I had seen same reports from reviewers across different games using this engine and I had experienced the same thing when playing Shadow Empires, however, I get ahead of myself. I was making good progress, I had checked my own progress at the end of summer and real life historic timelapse. I was going hex per hex with real life Operation Barbarossa. Everything seemed fine until the bugs showed their ugly head. I do not know if anyone had playtested it before, however game is currently unbeatable if you are going to get this bug. Group South will quickly run out of supply trucks if you do not reduce where most of your trucks are going. Group South is most stretched front due to Romania. This means that you have one front with one FSB, but have entirely different front to supply. This results in trucks running thousands of kilometers without telling you and quickly they all break and leaves your front without any trucks.

Supply system in general are extremely questionable. Supplies do not travel in a shortest possible route. Supply lines seem to be just one supply line drawn from one side. This was noticeable when taking Minsk, making supply base there and encircling enemies in in front of me. Supply trucks went from Minsk to Vilnius to supply troops across the river in the north and then they went all the way to my panzers across entire frontline. This resulted in thousands upon thousands of kilometers of ground which trucks have to cover which results in them quickly breaking down. These bugs are quite frequent as they happened twice in my play through and I suspect third such occurrence in group North where my base at the south of Leningrad was feeding trucks through Riga to reach troops on the few hexes near Estonia's border with Russia. The moment I changed my FSB from Riga to new one, my supply situation collapsed. 

Game seems unplayable in a long term due to bugs such as these. Supply bugs were noticed and in Shadow Empire and I read same thing about their other games too.

Now to the gimmick. It is just that, at first it seems interesting, however there is no depth in it. You make decisions to get more fuel, but you can't see how they impact you. Game does not give you any relevant information. You can't track what impact your decisions had. Statistics menu is surprisingly useless. It does not tell how much fuel you have, only how much it is delivered. It does not tell how much trucks you have, only how much trucks and trains front has. Game wishes you to make all those decisions however in practice you can't make them as you can't track any of them. Other decisions however are pointless. Like relocating supply bases and airfields. They will pop up randomly and will bother you as a bad AI will always suggest creating supply bases in sub-optimal positions. Sometimes however those events do not pop up, forcing you to wait turn after turn while your supply convoys are getting decimated. Choices themselves are just bad. It is never ending spam of meaningless logistical disputes which often have no impact on a game outside of balancing relationships. It is also very easy to balance relationships too as you will get events which raise relationships immensely with one or the other party while events usually are neutral relationship wise (net difference between reducing and increasing relationship is small). So, after initial good impression you will be pretty much with good to strong relationship with everybody while most of the decisions you will do be meaningless spam which are not even decisions, they are progression checks if you have political points. In addition, a lot of choices are RNG based. Nothing matters than a throw of a dice. It is extremely backwards and frustrating mechanic forcing player to quick load again and again until he gets outcome he wishes.

Game lacks any sort of detail. All units are reduced to generic templates. As this company has more advanced versions of this game with depth, it makes me wonder why they were so lazy not using what they had previously. Either way, game pays extremely little attention to details and be prepared to use German troops instead of Finnish ones.

Combat simulation is busted. You can attack with twice the number of more experienced and better trained troops against Soviet conscripts with higher readiness rating without them being properly digged in and lose 2000:0. Game calculates your casualties first and it seems to be little more complex than throw of a dice and multipliers. This results in combat which is often very unrealistic and frustrating to play when you can't mop up cut off battalions for several weeks with similar number of troops. In addition, mop ups often look like this. You lose 0 troops, enemy loses 50 000 troops along with all its tanks and equipment. 


Another problem is that you can't control your resources. Game does not tell you how many trains and trucks you have. It does not give control over which supply depots they should operate, you can't make their paths which sometimes leads into them bugging out and ruining your campaign. Once you ran out, this is it. Game expects you to cheat by pressing more resources button. It also gives events to give you more trucks at the cost of other divisions. However, as other divisions get supply by default, they are nothing more than extra 100 trucks per army group with only PP payments. I had checked, slow divisions had no impact due to cannibalising their supply networks. Game has extremely unrealistic system as you can't control nor track your resources. Truck minister sometimes tells me that I have over 300 trucks, but my army groups have to work with less than 100 of them. Terrible interface and information obscurantism results in a broken game where you can't tell if it is your fault or game just bugged out. Especially, if you ever go to 0, you will never have more trucks. No matter if you repair them, if your army group sits idly for a month. This is it. You are done and trucks only can raise through specifics events which are RNG based.

Game also does not handle logistics at all. There isn't any reinforcements, just waves while Russians are always reinforcing. You can constantly score 5 points in pretty much everything while your logistical line being broken for months. I was logistics master with army group South being stuck for a month without drop of fuel. 

The final nail to the coffin is that game itself is unrealistic at all. I do not expect in depth simulation, but AI does not play by the same rules at all. It ignores out of supply penalties and sometimes will go rampage through your back lines despite being cut off. AI will retain some fighting capacity while you units do not. AI will raise ton of conscripts which are side grade to Soviet infantry. So millions upon millions of good troops out of nowhere. AI form battalions just before frontlines. I wanted to break through their lines, but next turn it was tripled reinforced both in frontlines and formed a solid second line out of nowhere across entirety of that sector. AI cheats heavily and does not even attempt to hide it. It is just not fun to play against such opponent which you encircle every time, destroy majority of their army every few turns when your panzers operate and leave entire front wide open only to see it being reformed a turn later with troops appearing out of nowhere. It would be fine if you could keep doing that, sadly, the very premise of managing logistics of campaign are shallow, bugged and broken which will not allow to repeat this frustrating battle.

This is, without any doubt, by far the best strategic level wargame I have played during the last 44 years (I am 59).  You are not a leader that operates in a vacuum: you are involved in a complex sereis of relations with your superiors and subordinates that gives a very human, realistic, feeling to the game. How you develop those interactions is key to your battlefield performance. Logistics are smoothly modelled in an effective and not intrusive way. This game manages to strike the perfect balance between realism and playability imho.

The game is more on the hard side, but has good in built tutorial videos. 
Also i really like the logistic sytem. The scope of the game is a bit limited but you can add more scenarios with mods. Price is a bit much but worth for fans who look for a challanging hex war game

Tired to give the game a good amount of time but just found myself feeling frustrated and irritated at the micromanagement of decisions...

On top of that the "Political point" system that they use as a limited strategic resource that you have to ration in order to make the decisions mentioned above just makes the game irritating and unrealistic. 

I get that the developers are trying to create a sense of having to balance limited resources to achieve military goals - but it makes not sense that you can't relocate supply bases or fix trucks  /allocate trains etc if you have run out of Political points that were required to make a decision about moving an air field.....

It would have been much better to keep fuel and repairs etc separate; perhaps allow some kind of prioritisation of which fronts get priority from a limited available throughput. 

Ultimately the underlying game design needs a major rework to become enjoyable; for me any way.
